messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kai Ahina, a seasoned combat pilot from Hawaiian descent, had always been defined by his fearlessness in the skies. But it was on a routine training mission three years ago that his life took a drastic turn. As he banked hard to avoid a collision with another aircraft, Kai's plane stalled and plummeted towards the ground. He managed to regain control just inches from disaster, but the incident left an indelible mark. The memory of those moments still haunted him – the feeling of weightlessness, the screech of metal straining against gravity. Since then, Kai couldn't shake off the sense that he'd never be able to feel normal emotions again. He felt numb, like a part of him had been left behind in that near-fatal plunge. His wife, Lehua, would try to talk to him about their plans for retirement, but Kai just went through the motions, feeling like an imposter in his own life. As he navigated his daily routine, Kai found himself constantly on guard, scanning his surroundings for potential threats. He'd always been vigilant as a pilot, but this was different – now it felt like a reflex he couldn't shake off. At home, he'd position himself near the door, feeling more secure with an escape route mapped out in his mind. His wife would tease him about being "always ready to scramble," but Kai knew she didn't understand – for him, it wasn't just about being prepared; it was about survival. Kai's sense of self had taken a hit as well. He used to define himself by his fearlessness and skill in the cockpit, but now he felt lost and uncertain. Simple tasks like grocery shopping or attending social gatherings made him feel anxious and on edge. He'd tell Lehua that he didn't know who he was anymore – not the confident pilot he once was, nor a man content with quieter pursuits. As Kai struggled to reconcile his past and present selves, his perception of threat intensified. He became convinced that danger lurked around every corner, waiting to pounce. The thought sent him spiraling into worst-case scenarios: a home invasion, a catastrophic medical emergency, or even another near-fatal accident. His mind racing with escape routes and contingency plans, Kai felt like he was living in a perpetual state of high alert. Lehua had grown increasingly concerned about Kai's condition, urging him to seek help. At first, Kai resisted – what could anyone do to fix this? But as the months dragged on, even his beloved flying became too much to bear. The weight of his Negative Appraisals had created a self-perpetuating cycle: he felt like damaged goods, and that very feeling made the world seem all the more treacherous. It was only when Kai's commanding officer sat him down for an informal chat – noticing a dip in his performance and a withdrawal from squadron activities – that Kai realized just how far he'd drifted. With Lehua's support, he finally agreed to seek help, hoping to rediscover the man he once was – or at least find a way to live with the person he'd become.
